reconcile.connective: Defenders argue the ban never reaches David's line: the legal "bastard" meant only the issue of Leviticus 18 incest, "entering the congregation" meant office or marriage, and the count to David lands exactly at the tenth generation.

discrepancy.connective: Steve Wells presses this exact tension, counting only nine generations from the "bastard" Pharez to David and arguing the king's line therefore breaches the ten-generation ban of Deuteronomy 23:2.

skeptic.name: Steve Wells
skeptic.work: The Skeptic's Annotated Bible ("How many generations must a bastard wait until his offspring can enter the congregation of the Lord?")
skeptic.attribution: Steve Wells, The Skeptic's Annotated Bible, contra/bastard.html (1999-2026)

excerpts.excerpt_text: By bastards here the Jewish writers understand, not all that were born of fornication, or out of marriage, but all the issue of those incestuous mixtures which are forbidden, Lev. 18. … By this rule Jephthah, though the son of a harlot, a strange woman (Jdg 11:1, Jdg 11:2), yet was not a bastard in the sense of this law.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Narrows the legal 'bastard' (mamzer) to issue of Lev 18 incest, not all illegitimacy — undercutting the contradiction's assumption that David's descent through Pharez triggers the ban; the Jephthah case shows even a harlot's son escapes the category.

excerpts.excerpt_text: the Jews commonly interpret it of one that is born of any of those incestuous copulations forbidden in Lev 18:1 … yet according to the Jewish writers there were ways and means by which their posterity became legitimate
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Same scope-limiting reading of the term plus the explicit claim that the posterity could be legitimated — both directly answer how a barred line could still produce David within ten generations.

excerpts.excerpt_text: Either to bear office, or to marry a wife.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Defines 'enter the congregation' as bearing office or marrying an Israelite, not appearing in a lineage — so the prohibition does not bear on the genealogical descent the contradiction tallies.

pd_work.resource: John Gill, Exposition of the Entire Bible (1746-63), on Deuteronomy 23:2 and Matthew 1:3
pd_work.author: John Gill
pd_work.note: Gill treats this passage directly: he restricts the 'bastard' of Deut 23:2 to the issue of Leviticus 18 incest, notes the rabbinic means by which such posterity 'became legitimate,' and separately defends Pharez's place in the Matthean genealogy of the Messiah.
